title: London arrival, Ken Colyer's club and sitting in with British bands
summary: The crowd and brass band at the London station, a jam session at Colyer's club, and sitting in with Alan Yates, Rudy Marcellus and Chris Barber.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Did they have a sign up to know that they were welcoming you or something?

Well, yeah, they was all hollering, George Lewis, you know, and they had signs and they played. So when we got in, when they got to playing, when the ship landed, they came on the ship and it happened to be Chris Barbara and his band. And so anyway, well, that was fine. And we talked with them and we came on off the ship. It'd take a little time, you know, because we came off the ship. So that night we went where these fellows were playing at. And they played real good. So we left there. We left that Sunday and went into London. And when we got to London, the train got in there about 4.30 or something to 5 that evening. And when we get there, they had police. They came back there and they helped us back, you know. And I didn't know what was happening. I said, well, I wonder what's the matter. We, you know, they kept us there about 25, 30 minutes and it was cold out there, you know. So they said, all right, you know, before. So they said, all right, y'all can come on now. And the police, well, we did get to the, to where you go out the station. It looked like Carnival Day out there. And it had so many people and they all was on top of sheds and buildings and the police. They must have had about 25 or 30 police that were trying to get us through the crowd. And they had a brass band out there playing nothing but New Orleans tunes like we play on parades here. And it was Kemp Kaya. They had a brass band about 12, 14 pieces. And they was out there playing all these New Orleans tunes. And these people was clapping and howling. A shed fell in with some people.

Yeah, yes. The ambulance taking one or two to the, to the hospital. But I learned that there wasn't, nothing too serious. So I was glad for that. And the ambulance couldn't, the crowd was so, the ambulance couldn't pass by. This was brushing up against the people, moving and blowing to get out, you know. And we had a time getting out there. And I never saw so many photographers before in my life. It looked like they had 200 or more there. And they were taking pictures in the newspapers. And they were always full of the doors. Always full of that next stair and Joyce Lewis and the shed falling in. And well it was a wonderful center. I felt, I really felt good because this band was playing. That's like the New Orleans band's place on the parades here. And it was quite a surprise, you know. To hear them play all those marching tunes and play all these spiritual things. So that night we went out to Ken Kiley's club and they had some, oh it was crowded. You couldn't move in there. Did they have dancing there too? They have dancing, yeah they have dancing. They have dancing in there, but it was so crowded that night nobody couldn't dance because the people could, you couldn't move, you know. So I sat in and played with them, played a couple of pieces. Well everybody sat in a while with the exception of George. And we went to a place they called the, let's see what they call that, it's a little, the cottage they called it. The cottage. But we went there and they had a jam session there. Well they had all kinds of musicians. They had modern and jazz musicians and then we all sit and we played there until time for that, from the Stop the Music thing. Then I went out and played with this fellow, his name is Alan Yates. And they had a wonderful band. They had a real good band. They had a clarinet player there. He was a wonderful clarinet player there. Then they had a vibraphone player there. He was a subtle man. But man, that man could play some vibraphones. He could play vibraphones and he was so happy with playing. It was good for me to look at him play. And I sat there and I played with them quite a while and I went about 15 miles out and I sat in with another band. I don't know the name of the band. I don't know the name of the band, but the fellow, his name was Rudy Marcellus. He's from New Orleans. And he's kin to this Marcellus who's got this tourist code up here. And his cousins are very, very wonderful pianist. And he plays tenor, alto, clarinet, bass, and all the instruments he plays, all the instruments, real good. He's a good musician. And he told me that's his cousin. So anyway, I sit there and played with them. And now he's playing guitar and singing the blues. And when they left here he didn't play anything. He said he learned it since he'd been in England. He said he went over there with a ballet show. And he stayed over there. Then I met up and we played four concerts with Ken Kaya's band. And I think we played three with Chris Barber's band. And with Chris Barber's band they came over here in the swap.
They may still be here. I don't know.

Yeah, they may because they told me they was coming to New Orleans. They were coming here to see me. And they asked me where you were and I gave them your address. And they said they were coming by to see you.
